paras: The lynching of John Humphreys took place at Asheville, North Carolina, in the early morning of 15 July 1888, when a band of twenty-five to forty masked men broke into the county jail, took out the Black prisoner and hanged him to a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and was hanged before any trial. The Charlotte Democrat called it the first lynching known in Western North Carolina, and the Asheville dispatch was reprinted across the country.

On the afternoon of 14 July a rumor reached Asheville that Sallie Kate Parker, a white girl of 13, had been assaulted by a Black man in the northern suburbs of the city. According to the dispatch, she had been waylaid in a hollow in the woods on her way home from town and choked, and her throat and face were torn. Police searched the town and country, and about 9 o'clock that night they arrested John Humphreys.

The girl had described her attacker as wearing a striped shirt and going barefoot, and the dispatch said Humphreys had changed into a white shirt and shoes. He was made to put the striped shirt back on and was brought before the girl, who was reported to have identified him at once. He was held first in the city calaboose, but as "whispers of lynching" spread he was moved at 1 a.m. to the steel cage of the county jail.

About 3:15 a.m., by most versions, or 2:15 a.m. by the Charlotte Democrat's, the masked men entered the jail before Deputy Sheriff James Worley, who had charge of it, knew they were there. Worley seized a gun and fired on them from the top of the steps, and the mob answered with "a shower of bullets," though no one was reported hurt. Overpowered, he refused to give up the combination of the cage lock, so the mob tore the cage apart with sledgehammers and crowbars, a task that took about an hour.

The men then took Humphreys out and hanged him to a tree about a quarter of a mile from the jail, within the city limits. Once freed, Worley rang the fire bell and led a posse after the mob but was eluded, and the Charlotte Democrat reported that the body was found hanging "in view of the city and the mountain side above." A rumor carried in the dispatch held that Humphreys had confessed before he was hanged.

No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the mob or a grand-jury inquiry appears in the coverage. The Charlotte Democrat's version added, without a source, that the crowd "was partly made up of negroes" and that Humphreys was "a bad man from Spartanburg, S. C."

The account that circulated was a single Asheville dispatch, printed in full by the New York Sun on 16 July and by the Atlanta Constitution on 17 July, and condensed into telegram briefs in Arkansas, Mississippi, Minnesota, New Hampshire and West Virginia papers within the week.

Southern headlines treated the accusation as proven: the Atlanta Constitution ran the dispatch under the heading "A Season of Lynching Needed," after a first report predicting that the attacker would "find little mercy from his captors." The Newberry Herald and News headlined "A Negro Pays the Penalty for his Crime," and the Raleigh State Chronicle, which described the charge as an attempted rape, called the hanging "swift retribution." The New York Sun's heading, "A Girl Accuses him of Assault and a Mob Takes him in Hand," presented the charge as an accusation.

A different view came in October from "Karl Henry," a travel correspondent of the Essex County Herald of Guildhall, Vermont, whose earlier letter, dated Salisbury on 1 July, had him heading west toward the "Land of the Sky." He wrote that on the night before he reached Asheville "the jail was raided and a negro hung very informally to a poplar tree," naming neither the man nor the charge. He held that the act "should justify lynch law everywhere," yet asked, "Would they do so by a white man?"

accounts.label: Asheville wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A girl identified Humphreys after he was arrested; to forestall lynching he was moved to the jail's steel cage, but twenty-five to forty masked men overpowered the deputy, broke the cage and hanged him; a rumor said he confessed.

accounts.label: Charlotte Democrat version
accounts.gist: The same dispatch dated July 16, with the mob arriving about 2:15 a.m., the fire bell after 4 a.m., the body found within three hundred yards, and added claims that the crowd was partly Black and Humphreys was from Spartanburg.

accounts.label: Raleigh news item
accounts.gist: Humphreys attempted to rape a white girl near Asheville on Saturday and was lynched after lynchers broke open the jail that night.

accounts.label: Vermont travel correspondent
accounts.gist: The night before the writer reached Asheville the jail was raided and a Black man hanged to a poplar tree for an unnamed act.

framing.detail: The Atlanta Constitution headed the dispatch 'A Season of Lynching Needed' and predicted the attacker would 'find little mercy from his captors'.
The Newberry Herald and News headlined 'A Negro Pays the Penalty for his Crime', treating the accusation as proven.
The Raleigh State Chronicle called it 'swift retribution for the most heilish of hellish crimes'.
The New York Sun headlined 'A Girl Accuses him of Assault and a Mob Takes him in Hand', framing the charge as an accusation.
The Vermont correspondent said the act 'should justify lynch law everywhere' but asked 'Would they do so by a white man?'

conflicts.note: The Asheville dispatches, written on the scene, place the jail raid in the early hours of Sunday 15 July; the brief dates are condensations.
The Charlotte Democrat also says the fire bell rang a few minutes after 4 a.m.
All are accusations; no trial took place.
